title: Fluid Mechanics
description: Viscosity, hydrostatics, buoyancy, center of pressure, continuity, Bernoulli and Pitot tubes, Reynolds number, friction factor, head loss, drag scaling.

cards.title: A liquid has density $850\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$. What is its specific gravity?
cards.body:
$0.85$.

**Specific gravity** is $\mathrm{SG} = \rho/\rho_{\text{water}}$, with $\rho_{\text{water}} = 1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ (at $4\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$). It's dimensionless.

Example: specific weight $\gamma = \rho g$ in $\mathrm{N/m^3}$. Water has $\gamma \approx 9.81\,\mathrm{kN/m^3}$; this liquid has $850(9.81) \approx 8.34\,\mathrm{kN/m^3}$.
Watch out: SG has no units, but density and specific weight do.
cards.searchQuery: specific gravity of a liquid relative to water density

cards.title: What does the no-slip condition say about a viscous fluid in contact with a solid surface?
cards.body:
The fluid sticks to the surface: its velocity relative to the surface is zero.

At a stationary wall, $u = 0$. This creates a steep velocity gradient near walls (the **boundary layer**), which gives the wall shear stress $\tau_w = \mu\,(du/dy)_{\text{wall}}$, friction drag and pipe head loss.

Watch out: inviscid (Bernoulli) analyses can't satisfy no-slip; they allow slip at walls.
Key idea: viscosity plus no-slip is what makes real flows lose energy.
cards.searchQuery: no-slip condition fluid velocity at solid wall boundary layer

cards.title: Oil ($\mu = 0.1\,\mathrm{Pa\cdot s}$) fills a $2\,\mathrm{mm}$ gap between a fixed wall and a plate moving at $0.4\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Shear stress on the plate in Pa (linear velocity profile)?
cards.body:
$20\,\mathrm{Pa}$.

**Newton's law of viscosity:** $\tau = \mu\,\dfrac{du}{dy}$. No-slip makes the velocity go from $0$ to $0.4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ across the gap, so $\dfrac{du}{dy} = \dfrac{0.4}{0.002} = 200\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $\tau = 0.1(200) = 20\,\mathrm{Pa}$.

Example: $1\,\mathrm{Pa\cdot s} = 1\,\mathrm{N\cdot s/m^2} = 1\,\mathrm{kg/(m\cdot s)}$.
Watch out: convert the gap to meters before dividing.
cards.searchQuery: Newton law of viscosity shear stress plate moving gap oil

cards.title: Kinematic viscosity $\nu$ equals the dynamic viscosity $\mu$ divided by what?
cards.body:
Density: $\nu = \mu/\rho$, in $\mathrm{m^2/s}$.

At $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$: water $\nu \approx 1.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$, air $\nu \approx 1.5\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$. Air's $\nu$ is about $15\times$ water's even though its $\mu$ is about $55\times$ smaller, because air is about $830\times$ less dense.

Tip: $1\,\mathrm{stoke} = 1\,\mathrm{cm^2/s} = 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$.
Key idea: $\nu$ measures how fast momentum diffuses through the fluid.
cards.searchQuery: kinematic viscosity definition mu over rho units m2/s

cards.title: As temperature rises, what happens to the viscosity of a liquid, and of a gas?
cards.body:
Liquid: decreases. Gas: increases.

**Liquid** viscosity comes mainly from cohesive forces between molecules, which weaken as the molecules move faster. **Gas** viscosity comes from molecular collisions carrying momentum between layers, which intensify with temperature.

Example: motor oil thins out when hot, while air gets slightly more viscous.
Watch out: pressure has little effect on the viscosity of either, except at extreme pressures.
cards.searchQuery: viscosity temperature dependence liquid decreases gas increases

cards.title: What is the gauge pressure at the bottom of a $10\,\mathrm{m}$ deep open tank of fresh water, in kPa to one decimal?
cards.body:
$98.1\,\mathrm{kPa}$ (gauge).

$P = P_{\text{atm}} + \rho g h$, so $P_{\text{gauge}} = \rho g h = (1000)(9.81)(10) = 98{,}100\,\mathrm{Pa}$. Absolute: $\approx 101.3 + 98.1 = 199.4\,\mathrm{kPa}$ at sea level.

Key idea: pressure depends only on depth, not on the container's shape.
Watch out: $P_{\text{abs}} = P_{\text{atm}} + P_{\text{gauge}}$; below atmospheric, $P_{\text{abs}} = P_{\text{atm}} - P_{\text{vac}}$.
cards.searchQuery: hydrostatic gauge pressure rho g h depth of water tank

cards.title: A wooden block of density $600\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ floats in fresh water. What fraction of its volume is submerged?
cards.body:
$0.6$ ($60\%$).

**Archimedes:** the buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid, $F_B = \rho_{\text{fluid}}\,g\,V_{\text{sub}}$, acting up through the centroid of the displaced volume. Floating means $F_B = W$, so $\rho_w V_{\text{sub}} = \rho_b V$ and $V_{\text{sub}}/V = \rho_b/\rho_w$.

Watch out: $F_B$ uses the **fluid's** density and the submerged volume, not the body's.
cards.searchQuery: Archimedes principle floating block fraction submerged density ratio

cards.title: A vertical rectangular gate $3\,\mathrm{m}$ tall has its top edge at the water's free surface. At what depth, in meters, does the resultant hydrostatic force act?
cards.body:
$2\,\mathrm{m}$ deep ($\tfrac{2}{3}$ of the height), below the centroid at $1.5\,\mathrm{m}$.

The magnitude uses the centroid depth: $F_R = \rho g\,h_C A$. The location (gauge pressure) is $y_P = y_C + \dfrac{I_{xx,C}}{y_C A} = 1.5 + \dfrac{b(3)^3/12}{1.5(3b)} = 2\,\mathrm{m}$.

Key idea: on any non-horizontal plane surface the **center of pressure** lies below the centroid, approaching it as the surface goes deeper.
cards.searchQuery: center of pressure vertical rectangular gate hydrostatic force depth

cards.title: Water flows at $2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in a $10\,\mathrm{cm}$ diameter pipe that narrows to $5\,\mathrm{cm}$. What is the velocity in the narrow section, in m/s?
cards.body:
$8\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Incompressible **continuity**: $Q = A_1V_1 = A_2V_2$, so $V_2 = V_1\left(\dfrac{D_1}{D_2}\right)^2 = 2(2)^2 = 8\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Watch out: halving the diameter quarters the area, so the velocity rises $4\times$, not $2\times$.
Tip: for compressible flow, conserve the mass flow rate $\dot{m} = \rho A V$ instead.
cards.searchQuery: continuity equation pipe contraction velocity A1V1 = A2V2

cards.title: What four assumptions must hold to use the Bernoulli equation $\dfrac{P}{\rho} + \dfrac{V^2}{2} + gz = \text{constant}$?
cards.body:
Steady, incompressible, frictionless flow, applied along a streamline.

1. Steady flow
2. Incompressible flow
3. Negligible friction (viscous effects)
4. Applied along a **streamline**

There must also be no pump, turbine or heat transfer between the two points.

Watch out: it fails in boundary layers, in long pipes with friction and across a pump or fan; use the energy equation with head loss $h_L$ there.
cards.searchQuery: Bernoulli equation assumptions steady incompressible frictionless streamline

cards.title: A Pitot-static tube in air ($\rho = 1.2\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$) reads stagnation minus static pressure $= 240\,\mathrm{Pa}$. What is the air speed, in m/s?
cards.body:
$20\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Apply Bernoulli from the free stream to the stagnation point ($V = 0$): $P_0 = P + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2$, so $V = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(P_0 - P)}{\rho}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(240)}{1.2}} = \sqrt{400} = 20\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Watch out: use the density of the **flowing fluid** (air), not that of the manometer liquid.
cards.searchQuery: Pitot-static tube air speed stagnation pressure minus static pressure

cards.title: Water ($\nu = 1.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$) flows at $0.1\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in a $2\,\mathrm{cm}$ diameter pipe. What is the Reynolds number?
cards.body:
$2000$, so laminar.

$\mathrm{Re} = \dfrac{VD}{\nu} = \dfrac{\rho V D}{\mu} = \dfrac{(0.1)(0.02)}{10^{-6}} = 2000$, the ratio of **inertial to viscous** forces.

For circular pipes: laminar for $\mathrm{Re} \lesssim 2300$, transitional from about $2300$ to $4000$, turbulent for $\mathrm{Re} \gtrsim 4000$.
Watch out: these limits are approximate; transition depends on disturbances, wall roughness and vibration.
cards.searchQuery: Reynolds number pipe flow laminar turbulent VD over nu

cards.title: What is the Darcy friction factor $f$ for fully developed laminar flow in a circular pipe?
cards.body:
$f = \dfrac{64}{\mathrm{Re}}$.

In laminar flow it doesn't depend on wall roughness. In turbulent flow, $f$ depends on $\mathrm{Re}$ and the relative roughness $\varepsilon/D$ (Colebrook equation or Moody chart).

Watch out: the **Fanning** friction factor is $\tfrac{1}{4}$ of Darcy's ($16/\mathrm{Re}$), so check which one a chart or formula uses.
cards.searchQuery: Darcy friction factor laminar flow 64/Re circular pipe

cards.title: Darcy–Weisbach equation: head loss $h_L$ in a pipe of length $L$, diameter $D$, mean velocity $V$ and friction factor $f$?
cards.body:
$h_L = f\,\dfrac{L}{D}\,\dfrac{V^2}{2g}$, in meters of fluid.

As a pressure drop, $\Delta P_L = \rho g\,h_L = f\,\dfrac{L}{D}\,\dfrac{\rho V^2}{2}$. It's valid for laminar and turbulent flow.

Example: laminar ($f = 64/\mathrm{Re}$): $h_L \propto V$. Fully rough turbulent ($f$ constant): $h_L \propto V^2$.
Tip: at a fixed flow rate in fully rough flow, $h_L \propto 1/D^5$, so a slightly bigger pipe cuts losses a lot.
cards.searchQuery: Darcy-Weisbach equation head loss f L/D V^2/2g pipe

cards.title: What is the hydraulic diameter of a noncircular duct, and what does it reduce to for a circular pipe and for a square duct of side $a$?
cards.body:
$D_h = \dfrac{4A_c}{p}$, where $A_c$ is the flow area and $p$ the wetted perimeter.

Circle: $\dfrac{4(\pi D^2/4)}{\pi D} = D$. Square: $\dfrac{4a^2}{4a} = a$.

Use $D_h$ in place of $D$ in $\mathrm{Re}$ and the Darcy–Weisbach equation.
Watch out: laminar flow in noncircular ducts has its own $f\,\mathrm{Re}$ value (about $57$ for a square duct instead of $64$).
cards.searchQuery: hydraulic diameter noncircular duct 4A/p wetted perimeter

cards.title: Drag force $F_D = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2 C_D A$. If the speed doubles with $C_D$ unchanged, by what factor does the drag force change?
cards.body:
$4\times$ (it quadruples).

$F_D \propto V^2$, and the power needed to overcome drag, $F_D V$, rises $8\times$.

Watch out: $A$ is the frontal area for blunt bodies (cars, spheres) but the planform area for wings and plates parallel to the flow.
Tip: $C_D$ itself varies with $\mathrm{Re}$, so the $V^2$ scaling assumes $C_D$ stays roughly constant.
cards.searchQuery: drag force scaling with speed squared drag coefficient

cards.title: How does a fluid differ from a solid in its response to a shear stress?
cards.body:
A fluid deforms **continuously** under any applied shear stress, however small.

A solid deforms a finite amount and then resists. A fluid at rest can't sustain any shear stress, which is why static fluid pressure acts equally in all directions.

Example: water, air and oil are fluids; so are honey and toothpaste, which just flow slowly.
Key idea: this is the definition, and it applies to both liquids and gases.
cards.searchQuery: fluid definition continuous deformation under shear stress

cards.title: What is the density of fresh water at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, in $\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ to the nearest whole number?
cards.body:
$998\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.

Water is densest near $4\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($\approx 1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$). Between $0$ and $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ its density changes by less than $0.5\%$, so $1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ is fine for most problems.

Tip: use $\rho = 1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ unless the problem gives a more precise value.
Watch out: seawater is denser, about $1025\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.
cards.searchQuery: density of fresh water at 20 C kg/m3

cards.title: What is the specific weight $\gamma$ of fresh water in kN/m³ to two decimals? Use $\rho = 1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ and $g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
cards.body:
$9.81\,\mathrm{kN/m^3}$.

**Specific weight** is weight per unit volume: $\gamma = \rho g = (1000)(9.81) = 9810\,\mathrm{N/m^3}$.

In English units, water is about $62.4\,\mathrm{lbf/ft^3}$.
Watch out: $\gamma$ ($\mathrm{N/m^3}$) is not the same as $\rho$ ($\mathrm{kg/m^3}$); mixing them up changes answers by a factor of $g$.
cards.searchQuery: specific weight of water gamma rho g kN/m3

cards.title: What is the SI unit of dynamic viscosity $\mu$, written in terms of pascals?
cards.body:
Pa·s (pascal-second).

$1\,\mathrm{Pa\cdot s} = 1\,\mathrm{N\cdot s/m^2} = 1\,\mathrm{kg/(m\cdot s)}$.

It comes from $\mu = \tau/(du/dy)$: $\mathrm{Pa}$ divided by $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
Tip: the older CGS unit, the poise, is $0.1\,\mathrm{Pa\cdot s}$; water is about $1\,\mathrm{cP}$.
cards.searchQuery: dynamic viscosity SI unit Pa s newton second per square meter

cards.title: What is the dynamic viscosity of water at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, in mPa·s to two decimals?
cards.body:
$1.00\,\mathrm{mPa\cdot s}$ ($1.002\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Pa\cdot s}$, about $1\,\mathrm{cP}$).

Air at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is about $1.8\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{Pa\cdot s}$, roughly $55$ times smaller.

Why: dividing by density gives the kinematic viscosity, $\nu = \mu/\rho \approx 1.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$.
Tip: water's viscosity drops by more than half between $0$ and $50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
cards.searchQuery: viscosity of water at 20 C mPa s centipoise

cards.title: What type of non-Newtonian fluid becomes less viscous as the shear rate increases, like ketchup or paint?
cards.body:
A shear-thinning (pseudoplastic) fluid.

Its apparent viscosity falls as the shear rate rises, so it flows more easily when stirred or squeezed.

Example: **dilatant** (shear-thickening) fluids do the opposite, as with cornstarch in water.
Watch out: a Newtonian fluid has a constant $\mu$; in non-Newtonian fluids shear stress is not proportional to $du/dy$.
cards.searchQuery: shear thinning pseudoplastic fluid viscosity decreases with shear rate

cards.title: Capillary rise in a small vertical tube of radius $R$: what is the height $h$ in terms of surface tension $\sigma$, contact angle $\theta$, density $\rho$ and $g$?
cards.body:
$h = \dfrac{2\sigma\cos\theta}{\rho g R}$.

It comes from balancing the vertical surface-tension force, $2\pi R\,\sigma\cos\theta$, against the weight of the raised column, $\rho g\,\pi R^2 h$.

Example: water in clean glass has $\theta \approx 0$, so it rises. Mercury in glass has $\theta > 90^\circ$, so $h$ is negative: it's depressed.
Key idea: the rise grows as the tube gets narrower, because $h \propto 1/R$.
cards.searchQuery: capillary rise formula surface tension contact angle tube radius

cards.title: Define the bulk modulus of elasticity $E_v$ of a fluid.
cards.body:
$E_v = -V\,\dfrac{dP}{dV} = \rho\,\dfrac{dP}{d\rho}$, in Pa.

It measures resistance to compression: the pressure increase needed per unit fractional decrease in volume.

Example: water has $E_v \approx 2.2\,\mathrm{GPa}$, so a $0.1\%$ volume decrease needs about $2.2\,\mathrm{MPa}$.
Key idea: a large $E_v$ means nearly incompressible, which is why liquids are usually treated as constant-density.
cards.searchQuery: bulk modulus of elasticity fluid compressibility definition water

cards.title: What is cavitation, and why is it a problem?
cards.body:
Vapor bubbles form where the local pressure drops to the liquid's **vapor pressure**.

When the bubbles are carried to higher-pressure regions they collapse violently, causing noise, vibration and surface erosion (pitting) of pumps, propellers and valves.

Example: it can start at a pump inlet or at a high-speed throat where Bernoulli says $P$ falls.
Tip: warmer liquids have higher vapor pressure, so they cavitate more easily.
cards.searchQuery: cavitation vapor pressure bubble collapse pump damage

cards.title: Below roughly what Mach number can gas flow be treated as incompressible (density change under about $5\%$)?
cards.body:
$\mathrm{Ma} \approx 0.3$.

The density change in a flow is about $\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{Ma}^2$, so at $\mathrm{Ma} = 0.3$ it's about $4$ to $5\%$.

Example: air at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ has a speed of sound near $343\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so $\mathrm{Ma} = 0.3$ is about $100\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
Key idea: below this, air flows like a liquid for most purposes; Bernoulli with constant $\rho$ works.
cards.searchQuery: Mach number 0.3 incompressible flow limit density change

cards.title: For a static fluid with $z$ measured upward, what is the hydrostatic pressure gradient $\dfrac{dP}{dz}$?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{dP}{dz} = -\rho g$.

Pressure increases as you go **down**. For constant density, $P_2 - P_1 = \rho g\,(z_1 - z_2) = \rho g\,\Delta h$ for a depth change $\Delta h$.

Why: a thin horizontal slab of fluid must be held up by the pressure difference across it, which balances its weight.
Watch out: for gases over large height changes, $\rho$ varies, so you can't use constant-density $\rho g h$.
cards.searchQuery: hydrostatic pressure gradient dP/dz = -rho g fluid at rest

cards.title: State Pascal's law for a fluid at rest.
cards.body:
A pressure change applied to an enclosed static fluid is transmitted undiminished to every point in the fluid and to its walls.

The pressure at a point is the same in all directions, and points at the same depth in one connected fluid have equal pressure.

Example: hydraulic jacks and brakes use it to multiply force.
Key idea: pressure, unlike force, is the same everywhere the fluid is connected at a given depth.
cards.searchQuery: Pascal law pressure transmitted undiminished static fluid

cards.title: A hydraulic lift's pistons have areas $10\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ and $200\,\mathrm{cm^2}$. A $100\,\mathrm{N}$ force acts on the small piston. What load can the large piston support, in N?
cards.body:
$2000\,\mathrm{N}$.

By Pascal's law the pressure is equal: $\dfrac{F_1}{A_1} = \dfrac{F_2}{A_2}$, so $F_2 = F_1\dfrac{A_2}{A_1} = 100(20) = 2000\,\mathrm{N}$.

Why: work is conserved, so the small piston must move $20\times$ farther than the large one.
Watch out: the force multiplication isn't free energy; the distance moved shrinks by the same factor.
cards.searchQuery: hydraulic lift force multiplication piston area ratio Pascal

cards.title: A standard atmosphere ($101.325\,\mathrm{kPa}$) supports a mercury column of what height, in mm to the nearest 10 mm? Use $\rho_{\mathrm{Hg}} = 13{,}600\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.
cards.body:
$760\,\mathrm{mm}$.

$h = \dfrac{P}{\rho g} = \dfrac{101{,}325}{(13{,}600)(9.81)} = 0.759\,\mathrm{m}$.

Mercury is used because its density is high, giving a manageable column; a water barometer would need about $10.3\,\mathrm{m}$.
Tip: $1\,\mathrm{atm} = 760\,\mathrm{mmHg} = 101.325\,\mathrm{kPa}$.
cards.searchQuery: mercury barometer height standard atmosphere 760 mm

cards.title: A mercury manometer ($13{,}600\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$) shows a $0.2\,\mathrm{m}$ level difference between a gas tank and the atmosphere. Gauge pressure of the gas, in kPa to one decimal?
cards.body:
$26.7\,\mathrm{kPa}$.

$P_{\text{gauge}} = \rho g h = (13{,}600)(9.81)(0.2) = 26{,}683\,\mathrm{Pa}$.

Why: a manometer reads pressure as the weight of a liquid column; the gas column is so light it's neglected.
Watch out: convert mmHg or cm of fluid to meters, and use the manometer fluid's density, not the density of the fluid in the pipe.
cards.searchQuery: U-tube mercury manometer gauge pressure rho g h kPa

cards.title: A tank has a flat horizontal bottom of $2\,\mathrm{m} \times 3\,\mathrm{m}$ under $4\,\mathrm{m}$ of fresh water. Hydrostatic (gauge) force on the bottom, in kN to the nearest whole number?
cards.body:
$235\,\mathrm{kN}$.

On a horizontal surface the pressure is uniform, so $F = \rho g h A = (1000)(9.81)(4)(6) = 235{,}440\,\mathrm{N}$.

Why: pressure depends only on depth, so the force on a flat bottom doesn't depend on the tank's shape above it.
Watch out: this is the gauge force; the atmosphere pushes on both sides of the bottom.
cards.searchQuery: hydrostatic force on horizontal tank bottom rho g h A

cards.title: A vertical rectangular gate, $2\,\mathrm{m}$ wide and $3\,\mathrm{m}$ tall, has its top edge at the water surface. Resultant hydrostatic force, in kN to one decimal?
cards.body:
$88.3\,\mathrm{kN}$.

$F_R = \rho g\,h_C A = (1000)(9.81)(1.5)(6) = 88{,}290\,\mathrm{N}$, where $h_C = 1.5\,\mathrm{m}$ is the centroid depth.

Key idea: the force equals the **average** pressure (the pressure at the centroid) times the area.
Watch out: using the bottom depth ($3\,\mathrm{m}$) instead of the centroid depth doubles the answer.
cards.searchQuery: hydrostatic force on submerged vertical rectangular plate centroid pressure

cards.title: For a submerged curved surface, how do you find the horizontal and vertical components of the hydrostatic force?
cards.body:
Horizontal: the force on the vertical projection of the surface. Vertical: the weight of the liquid directly above the surface.

The vertical component acts through the centroid of that liquid volume; the horizontal one acts at the center of pressure of the projection.

Why: the liquid column above (real or imagined) is in equilibrium, so it balances the surface's vertical force.
Tip: if the liquid is below the surface, use the weight of the imaginary liquid that would fill the volume above, and the vertical force points up.
cards.searchQuery: hydrostatic force curved surface horizontal vertical components projection

cards.title: A $0.002\,\mathrm{m^3}$ block of density $7800\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ is fully submerged in fresh water. Its apparent weight, in N to one decimal?
cards.body:
$133.4\,\mathrm{N}$.

Weight $W = \rho_b g V = (7800)(9.81)(0.002) = 153.0\,\mathrm{N}$. Buoyant force $F_B = \rho_w g V = (1000)(9.81)(0.002) = 19.6\,\mathrm{N}$.

Apparent weight $= W - F_B = 153.0 - 19.6 = 133.4\,\mathrm{N}$ (the scale reading if you hang it in the water).
Watch out: use the full volume in $F_B$ since the block is totally submerged.
cards.searchQuery: apparent weight submerged block buoyant force Archimedes calculation

cards.title: For a floating body to be stable against small rotations, is its metacenter $M$ above or below its center of gravity $G$?
cards.body:
Above.

The metacentric height $\overline{GM} = \overline{MB} - \overline{BG}$ must be positive. Then a small tilt creates a **restoring** moment from the shifted center of buoyancy.

If $M$ is below $G$, the tilt creates an overturning moment and the body capsizes.
Key idea: a wide hull raises $M$, which is why wide boats are stable but can roll quickly.
cards.searchQuery: metacenter metacentric height stability floating body above center of gravity

cards.title: The buoyant force acts through the centroid of the displaced volume. What is that point called?
cards.body:
The center of buoyancy.

It lies at the centroid of the **displaced** fluid volume, not necessarily at the body's own center of gravity.

Example: for a floating, partly submerged body it is the centroid of just the underwater part.
Tip: when a body tilts, the center of buoyancy moves because the underwater shape changes; this shift creates the restoring moment.
cards.searchQuery: center of buoyancy centroid of displaced volume

cards.title: Ice ($917\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$) floats in seawater ($1025\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$). What fraction of the ice's volume is submerged, to two decimals?
cards.body:
$0.89$ ($89\%$).

Floating: $\dfrac{V_{\text{sub}}}{V} = \dfrac{\rho_{\text{ice}}}{\rho_{\text{sea}}} = \dfrac{917}{1025} = 0.895$.

In fresh water the fraction is $917/1000 = 0.917$, so ice sits slightly lower there.
Key idea: about nine-tenths of an iceberg is below the waterline.
cards.searchQuery: iceberg fraction submerged ice density seawater floating

cards.title: What is a streamline?
cards.body:
A curve that's everywhere tangent to the local velocity vector at a given instant.

No fluid crosses a streamline. In **steady** flow, streamlines, pathlines and streaklines all coincide.

Example: in a pipe, streamlines run parallel to the wall; around a cylinder they bend and crowd where the flow speeds up.
Tip: closer streamline spacing means higher speed, since the same flow passes through a smaller gap.
cards.searchQuery: streamline definition tangent to velocity vector fluid flow

cards.title: What is the difference between steady flow and uniform flow?
cards.body:
Steady: nothing changes with **time** at a point. Uniform: nothing changes with **position** along the flow.

Water flowing through a long constant-diameter pipe at a constant rate is both. A converging nozzle at constant flow rate is steady but not uniform.

Example: a tank draining through a hole is unsteady, since the speed changes as the level drops.
Watch out: "steady" and "uniform" are independent properties; a flow can be one without the other.
cards.searchQuery: steady flow versus uniform flow fluid mechanics difference

cards.title: Which description of fluid motion, Eulerian or Lagrangian, observes the flow at fixed points in space as fluid passes through?
cards.body:
Eulerian.

The **Eulerian** approach defines fields like $\vec{V}(x, y, z, t)$ and $P(x, y, z, t)$. The **Lagrangian** approach follows individual fluid particles along their paths.

Why: following every particle in a flow is impractical, so most fluid mechanics, including control-volume analysis, uses the Eulerian view.
Tip: a weather map is Eulerian; a drifting weather balloon is Lagrangian.
cards.searchQuery: Eulerian versus Lagrangian description fluid flow fixed point

cards.title: Can a fluid particle accelerate in a steady flow? Explain.
cards.body:
Yes, through convective acceleration: its velocity changes as it moves to a new position.

For 1-D flow, $a = \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t} + u\,\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}$. In steady flow the first term is $0$, but $u\,\partial u/\partial x \ne 0$ wherever the speed varies along the path.

Example: water speeding up through a converging nozzle at constant flow rate has $u\,\partial u/\partial x > 0$.
Key idea: the full acceleration is the material derivative, $\dfrac{D\vec{V}}{Dt}$.
cards.searchQuery: convective acceleration steady flow nozzle material derivative

cards.title: Water flows at $3\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in a pipe of $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ inner diameter. Volume flow rate, in L/s to one decimal?
cards.body:
$5.9\,\mathrm{L/s}$.

$A = \dfrac{\pi D^2}{4} = \dfrac{\pi(0.05)^2}{4} = 1.963\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2}$, so $Q = VA = (3)(1.963\times10^{-3}) = 5.89\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3/s}$.

Tip: $1\,\mathrm{m^3/s} = 1000\,\mathrm{L/s}$.
Watch out: use the diameter in meters, and square it: $D = 5$ with $D$ in cm gives an answer $10^4$ times too large.
cards.searchQuery: volume flow rate Q = V A pipe diameter water liters per second

cards.title: Write the Bernoulli equation in head form, and name each term.
cards.body:
$\dfrac{P}{\rho g} + \dfrac{V^2}{2g} + z = H = \text{constant}$

The terms are the **pressure head**, the **velocity head** and the **elevation head**, each in meters of fluid.

Why: dividing the energy-per-mass form $\dfrac{P}{\rho} + \dfrac{V^2}{2} + gz$ by $g$ gives lengths.
Key idea: the sum is the **total head**; along a streamline in frictionless flow it can't change.
cards.searchQuery: Bernoulli equation head form pressure head velocity head elevation head

cards.title: A large open tank has a small hole $5\,\mathrm{m}$ below the water surface. What is the jet speed, in m/s to one decimal? (Neglect friction.)
cards.body:
$9.9\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

**Torricelli's law:** $V = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2(9.81)(5)} = \sqrt{98.1} = 9.90\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Why: Bernoulli between the surface (where $V \approx 0$, gauge $P = 0$) and the jet (gauge $P = 0$) gives $gh = V^2/2$.
Key idea: it's the speed of a body freely falling through the same height $h$.
cards.searchQuery: Torricelli law tank hole exit velocity sqrt(2gh) Bernoulli

cards.title: Water in a horizontal Venturi meter speeds up from $2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at the inlet to $6\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at the throat. Pressure drop from inlet to throat, in kPa?
cards.body:
$16\,\mathrm{kPa}$.

Horizontal Bernoulli: $P_1 - P_2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho\,(V_2^2 - V_1^2) = \tfrac{1}{2}(1000)(36 - 4) = 16{,}000\,\mathrm{Pa}$.

Why: the kinetic energy gained by the fluid comes from the pressure energy.
Tip: in a real Venturi meter, measuring $\Delta P$ and using continuity to eliminate one velocity gives the flow rate.
cards.searchQuery: Venturi meter pressure drop Bernoulli velocity increase throat

cards.title: What is the dynamic pressure $\tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2$ of water moving at $5\,\mathrm{m/s}$, in kPa to one decimal?
cards.body:
$12.5\,\mathrm{kPa}$.

$\tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(1000)(5)^2 = 12{,}500\,\mathrm{Pa}$.

The **stagnation pressure** is static plus dynamic: $P_0 = P + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2$, the pressure at the point where the flow is brought to rest.
Watch out: dynamic pressure is not an actual pressure on a moving fluid's walls; it's the extra pressure you'd get by stopping the flow.
cards.searchQuery: dynamic pressure 1/2 rho V squared water stagnation pressure

cards.title: The energy grade line (EGL) lies above the hydraulic grade line (HGL) by how much?
cards.body:
The velocity head, $\dfrac{V^2}{2g}$.

$\mathrm{HGL} = \dfrac{P}{\rho g} + z$ and $\mathrm{EGL} = \dfrac{P}{\rho g} + \dfrac{V^2}{2g} + z$.

Why: the HGL is where a piezometer tube would stand; the EGL is where a Pitot tube would stand.
Tip: with friction, the EGL slopes **downward** along the flow, falling by $h_L$; it rises only across a pump.
cards.searchQuery: energy grade line hydraulic grade line difference velocity head

cards.title: A pump moves $0.02\,\mathrm{m^3/s}$ of water through a head of $20\,\mathrm{m}$ with an overall efficiency of $80\%$. Shaft power required, in kW to one decimal?
cards.body:
$4.9\,\mathrm{kW}$.

Useful (water) power: $\rho g Q H = (1000)(9.81)(0.02)(20) = 3924\,\mathrm{W}$. Shaft power: $\dfrac{3924}{0.80} = 4905\,\mathrm{W}$.

Key idea: shaft power $= \dfrac{\rho g Q H}{\eta_{\text{pump}}}$; the pump needs more than the useful power.
Watch out: multiplying by $\eta$ instead of dividing gives the (smaller) useful power.
cards.searchQuery: pump shaft power rho g Q H over efficiency water head

cards.title: A water jet ($A = 10\,\mathrm{cm^2}$, $V = 10\,\mathrm{m/s}$) hits a stationary flat plate head-on and flows off sideways. Force on the plate, in N?
cards.body:
$100\,\mathrm{N}$.

Momentum balance: the jet loses all its momentum normal to the plate, so $F = \dot{m}V = \rho A V^2 = (1000)(0.001)(10)^2 = 100\,\mathrm{N}$.

Why: $\dot{m} = \rho A V = 10\,\mathrm{kg/s}$, and each kilogram loses $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ of normal velocity.
Watch out: if the plate moves with speed $V_p$, use the relative velocity $(V - V_p)$ in both the mass flow and the velocity change.
cards.searchQuery: water jet force on flat plate momentum equation rho A V squared

cards.title: What is the kinetic energy correction factor $\alpha$ for fully developed laminar flow in a circular pipe?
cards.body:
$\alpha = 2$.

$\alpha$ corrects the kinetic energy flux computed from the mean velocity: $\text{KE flux} = \alpha\,\dot{m}\,\dfrac{V_{\text{avg}}^2}{2}$.

For turbulent pipe flow the profile is flatter and $\alpha \approx 1.05$ (close to $1$), so it's usually set to $1$.
Watch out: in laminar flow, ignoring $\alpha$ underestimates the kinetic energy by half.
cards.searchQuery: kinetic energy correction factor alpha laminar pipe flow 2

cards.title: A Pitot tube in water reads a stagnation pressure $10\,\mathrm{kPa}$ above the static pressure. What is the flow speed, in m/s to one decimal?
cards.body:
$4.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

$V = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(P_0 - P)}{\rho}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(10{,}000)}{1000}} = \sqrt{20} = 4.47\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Key idea: the Pitot reading is the dynamic pressure, $\tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2$.
Watch out: convert kPa to Pa first, or the speed comes out $\sqrt{1000}$ too small.
cards.searchQuery: Pitot tube water flow speed stagnation pressure calculation

cards.title: Fully developed laminar flow in a circular pipe of radius $R$: what is the shape of the velocity profile $u(r)$?
cards.body:
Parabolic: $u(r) = u_{\max}\left(1 - \dfrac{r^2}{R^2}\right)$.

The speed is $u_{\max}$ at the centerline and $0$ at the wall (no-slip). The shear stress varies linearly from $0$ at the center to $\tau_w$ at the wall.

Why: it comes from balancing the pressure force on a fluid cylinder against the viscous shear on its surface.
Key idea: the profile stays the same shape along the pipe once the flow is fully developed.
cards.searchQuery: laminar pipe flow parabolic velocity profile Hagen-Poiseuille

cards.title: In fully developed laminar flow in a circular pipe, what is the ratio of the centerline velocity to the mean velocity?
cards.body:
$u_{\max}/V_{\text{avg}} = 2$.

Averaging the parabolic profile over the cross-section gives $V_{\text{avg}} = \tfrac{1}{2}u_{\max}$.

Example: if the mean velocity is $0.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$, the centerline speed is $1.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
Watch out: this holds for laminar flow only; turbulent profiles are flatter, with $u_{\max}/V_{\text{avg}}$ closer to $1.2$.
cards.searchQuery: laminar pipe flow centerline velocity twice average velocity

cards.title: Hagen–Poiseuille law: pressure drop $\Delta P$ for laminar flow rate $Q$ of a fluid of viscosity $\mu$ in a pipe of length $L$ and diameter $D$?
cards.body:
$\Delta P = \dfrac{128\,\mu L Q}{\pi D^4} = \dfrac{32\,\mu L V}{D^2}$.

It follows from integrating the parabolic velocity profile, and it's equivalent to $f = 64/\mathrm{Re}$ in the Darcy–Weisbach equation.

Key idea: $\Delta P \propto \mu L Q$ and, strongly, $\Delta P \propto 1/D^4$.
Watch out: use it only for laminar flow ($\mathrm{Re} \lesssim 2300$) and fully developed flow.
cards.searchQuery: Hagen-Poiseuille equation laminar pipe pressure drop 128 mu L Q

cards.title: In laminar pipe flow at a fixed flow rate, by what factor does the pressure drop increase if the diameter is halved?
cards.body:
$16\times$.

From Hagen–Poiseuille, $\Delta P \propto \dfrac{1}{D^4}$, and $\left(\dfrac{1}{1/2}\right)^4 = 16$.

Why: halving $D$ also quarters the area, so the velocity quadruples, and the friction term per unit length grows with $V/D^2$.
Tip: this strong dependence is why small tubes (needles, capillaries) resist flow so much more than larger ones.
cards.searchQuery: laminar flow pressure drop diameter halved factor 16 D^4

cards.title: The laminar hydrodynamic entry length in a pipe is $L_h \approx c\,\mathrm{Re}\,D$. What is the approximate coefficient $c$?
cards.body:
$c \approx 0.05$.

So at $\mathrm{Re} = 2000$, $L_h \approx 0.05(2000)D = 100D$.

The entrance region is where the **boundary layer** grows to fill the pipe, after which the velocity profile stops changing.
Tip: for turbulent flow, the entry length is much shorter, roughly $10D$, and depends only weakly on $\mathrm{Re}$.
cards.searchQuery: laminar hydrodynamic entry length 0.05 Re D pipe

cards.title: What is the Colebrook equation, and what is it used for?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{f}} = -2.0\log_{10}\!\left(\dfrac{\varepsilon/D}{3.7} + \dfrac{2.51}{\mathrm{Re}\sqrt{f}}\right)$

It gives the Darcy friction factor $f$ for **turbulent** flow in pipes from the Reynolds number and the relative roughness $\varepsilon/D$. The Moody chart is its graph.

Watch out: it's implicit in $f$, so solve by iteration (or use an explicit approximation such as Haaland).
Tip: start with the fully rough value ($\mathrm{Re} \to \infty$) as the first guess.
cards.searchQuery: Colebrook equation turbulent friction factor relative roughness Moody chart

cards.title: At very high Reynolds number in a rough pipe, the friction factor stops depending on $\mathrm{Re}$ and depends only on $\varepsilon/D$. What is this regime called?
cards.body:
Fully rough turbulent flow.

In the Moody chart this is the flat, right-hand part of each curve. There the head loss varies as $V^2$ because $f$ is constant.

Why: the viscous sublayer becomes thinner than the roughness bumps, so the bumps, not viscosity, control the wall drag.
Watch out: in a smooth pipe $f$ keeps decreasing slowly with $\mathrm{Re}$ and never becomes constant.
cards.searchQuery: fully rough turbulent flow Moody chart friction factor independent of Reynolds

cards.title: How is a minor (local) head loss from a fitting, bend or valve expressed using a loss coefficient $K_L$?
cards.body:
$h_L = K_L\,\dfrac{V^2}{2g}$

$K_L$ is a dimensionless, experimentally determined number for each fitting. The pressure drop is $\Delta P_L = K_L\,\dfrac{\rho V^2}{2}$.

Example: a fully open globe valve has a large $K_L$ (about $10$); a smooth well-rounded entrance has a small one.
Tip: add all the minor losses to the pipe friction loss, $h_{L,\text{total}} = \left(f\dfrac{L}{D} + \sum K_L\right)\dfrac{V^2}{2g}$.
cards.searchQuery: minor loss coefficient K V^2/2g fitting valve bend head loss

cards.title: Water flows at $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in a $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ pipe that suddenly expands to $10\,\mathrm{cm}$. Head loss at the expansion, in m to two decimals?
cards.body:
$0.46\,\mathrm{m}$.

$V_2 = V_1(D_1/D_2)^2 = 4\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = 1\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so $h_L = \dfrac{(V_1 - V_2)^2}{2g} = \dfrac{(3)^2}{2(9.81)} = 0.459\,\mathrm{m}$.

Equivalently, $K_L = \left(1 - \dfrac{A_1}{A_2}\right)^2 = 0.5625$ based on $V_1$, and $h_L = 0.5625\,\dfrac{16}{19.62}$.
Watch out: this loss arises because the fast jet mixes turbulently with the slower fluid; a gradual diffuser reduces it.
cards.searchQuery: sudden expansion head loss (V1 - V2)^2/2g pipe calculation

cards.title: What is the loss coefficient $K_L$ for a sharp-edged pipe entrance from a large reservoir (approximately)?
cards.body:
$K_L \approx 0.5$.

For a well-rounded entrance it falls to about $0.03$ and for a re-entrant (inward-projecting) pipe it rises to about $0.8$.

Why: the flow separates at the sharp corner and contracts into a vena contracta, then re-expands, dissipating energy.
Key idea: rounding the entrance is the cheapest way to cut this loss.
cards.searchQuery: sharp-edged pipe entrance loss coefficient K 0.5 reservoir

cards.title: What is the loss coefficient $K_L$ for a pipe discharging into a large reservoir (approximately)?
cards.body:
$K_L = 1$.

All of the pipe's kinetic energy, $V^2/2g$, is dissipated in the reservoir, so the loss is exactly one velocity head.

Watch out: if the pipe discharges as a free jet into air, there's no exit loss term; instead the jet carries kinetic energy $V^2/2g$ away.
Tip: in an energy equation between two reservoir surfaces, include both the entrance loss and the exit loss.
cards.searchQuery: pipe exit loss coefficient K = 1 discharge into reservoir velocity head

cards.title: A fitting with $K_L = 2$ is in a $0.05\,\mathrm{m}$ diameter pipe with $f = 0.025$. What length of straight pipe, in m, gives the same head loss?
cards.body:
$4\,\mathrm{m}$.

Equate $K_L\dfrac{V^2}{2g} = f\dfrac{L_{\text{eq}}}{D}\dfrac{V^2}{2g}$, so $L_{\text{eq}} = \dfrac{K_L D}{f} = \dfrac{(2)(0.05)}{0.025} = 4\,\mathrm{m}$.

Tip: this lets you treat fittings as extra pipe length when computing total losses.
Watch out: $L_{\text{eq}}$ depends on $f$ and $D$, so it isn't a universal constant for a fitting.
cards.searchQuery: equivalent length fitting K D over f straight pipe head loss

cards.title: For pipes connected in series, which quantity is the same in every pipe, and which quantity adds up?
cards.body:
The flow rate is the same; the head losses add.

$Q_1 = Q_2 = \cdots$ and $h_{L,\text{total}} = h_{L,1} + h_{L,2} + \cdots$

Why: there's one path, so mass conservation fixes $Q$, and energy loss accumulates along the way.
Key idea: the velocity in each pipe differs when the diameters differ, since $V = Q/A$.
cards.searchQuery: pipes in series same flow rate head losses add

cards.title: For pipes connected in parallel between two junctions, which quantity adds up, and which is the same across all branches?
cards.body:
The flow rates add; the head loss is the same across each branch.

$Q_{\text{total}} = Q_1 + Q_2 + \cdots$ and $h_{L,1} = h_{L,2} = \cdots$

Why: all branches connect the same two junctions, so they share the same pressure difference.
Tip: the branch with the lowest resistance (larger $D$, shorter $L$) carries the most flow.
cards.searchQuery: pipes in parallel flow rates add head loss equal branches

cards.title: Water flows at $2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ through a $0.1\,\mathrm{m}$ diameter, $100\,\mathrm{m}$ long pipe with $f = 0.02$. Head loss, in m to two decimals?
cards.body:
$4.08\,\mathrm{m}$.

$h_L = f\,\dfrac{L}{D}\,\dfrac{V^2}{2g} = (0.02)\dfrac{100}{0.1}\dfrac{(2)^2}{2(9.81)} = 20\,(0.2039) = 4.08\,\mathrm{m}$.

The velocity head is $V^2/2g = 4/19.62 = 0.204\,\mathrm{m}$, and the pipe is $1000$ diameters long.
Watch out: forgetting the $2$ in $2g$ doubles the answer.
cards.searchQuery: Darcy-Weisbach head loss calculation pipe water f L/D V^2/2g

cards.title: Water ($1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$) flows at $2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ through a horizontal $0.1\,\mathrm{m}$ diameter, $100\,\mathrm{m}$ long pipe with $f = 0.02$. Pressure drop, in kPa?
cards.body:
$40\,\mathrm{kPa}$.

$\Delta P = f\,\dfrac{L}{D}\,\dfrac{\rho V^2}{2} = (0.02)(1000)\dfrac{(1000)(4)}{2} = 40{,}000\,\mathrm{Pa}$.

Check: $\rho g\,h_L = (1000)(9.81)(4.08) \approx 40\,\mathrm{kPa}$.
Tip: for a horizontal, constant-diameter pipe, the pressure drop equals the friction pressure loss, since $\Delta z = 0$ and $\Delta V = 0$.
cards.searchQuery: pipe pressure drop Darcy-Weisbach horizontal pipe kPa calculation

cards.title: A pump must supply $0.01\,\mathrm{m^3/s}$ of water against a total head loss of $10\,\mathrm{m}$ (no elevation or pressure change). Hydraulic power delivered to the water, in W?
cards.body:
$981\,\mathrm{W}$.

$\dot{W} = \rho g Q h_L = (1000)(9.81)(0.01)(10) = 981\,\mathrm{W}$.

Why: the pump head must equal the head loss, $h_{\text{pump}} = h_L$, so the water gains energy at that rate.
Tip: divide by the pump-motor efficiency to get the electrical power drawn.
cards.searchQuery: pump power to overcome head loss rho g Q h_L watts

cards.title: A rectangular duct has a $4\,\mathrm{cm} \times 6\,\mathrm{cm}$ cross-section. What is its hydraulic diameter, in cm to one decimal?
cards.body:
$4.8\,\mathrm{cm}$.

$D_h = \dfrac{4A_c}{p} = \dfrac{4(4)(6)}{2(4 + 6)} = \dfrac{96}{20} = 4.8\,\mathrm{cm}$.

Use $D_h$ in $\mathrm{Re} = V D_h/\nu$ and in the Darcy–Weisbach equation for turbulent flow.
Watch out: the wetted perimeter is the full perimeter, $20\,\mathrm{cm}$, for a closed duct that's flowing full.
cards.searchQuery: hydraulic diameter rectangular duct 4A/p calculation

cards.title: In the Buckingham Pi theorem, a problem has $n$ variables expressed in $k$ primary dimensions. How many independent dimensionless groups $\Pi$ are there (in terms of $n$ and $k$)?
cards.body:
$n - k$.

Each $\Pi$ is a dimensionless product of the variables; the relationship among the variables can then be written as $\Pi_1 = f(\Pi_2, \dots, \Pi_{n-k})$.

Example: drag on a sphere has $n = 5$ variables ($F_D$, $\rho$, $V$, $D$, $\mu$) and $k = 3$ dimensions (M, L, T), giving $2$ groups: $C_D$ and $\mathrm{Re}$.
Tip: choose $k$ repeating variables that together include all the dimensions but can't form a dimensionless group.
cards.searchQuery: Buckingham Pi theorem number of dimensionless groups n minus k

cards.title: The Froude number $\mathrm{Fr} = \dfrac{V}{\sqrt{gL}}$ is the ratio of inertial forces to which other force?
cards.body:
Gravity.

It matters whenever gravity drives the flow or a free surface is present: ship waves, open channels, spillways.

Key idea: for $\mathrm{Fr} = 1$ in open channels (critical flow), the flow speed equals the speed of surface waves, $\sqrt{gy}$.
Tip: in ship-model testing, equal $\mathrm{Fr}$ (not equal $\mathrm{Re}$) is usually matched.
cards.searchQuery: Froude number ratio inertial to gravity forces free surface

cards.title: The Mach number $\mathrm{Ma} = V/c$ is the flow speed divided by what?
cards.body:
The local speed of sound, $c$.

Regimes: subsonic $\mathrm{Ma} < 1$, sonic $\mathrm{Ma} = 1$, supersonic $\mathrm{Ma} > 1$. Compressibility effects are important above about $\mathrm{Ma} \approx 0.3$.

Example: in air at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $c \approx 343\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so a jet at $686\,\mathrm{m/s}$ is at $\mathrm{Ma} = 2$.
Watch out: $c$ depends on temperature, so the same speed can be a different Mach number at altitude.
cards.searchQuery: Mach number flow speed divided by speed of sound

cards.title: The Weber number $\mathrm{We} = \dfrac{\rho V^2 L}{\sigma}$ is the ratio of inertial forces to which other force?
cards.body:
Surface tension.

It matters for droplets, bubbles, sprays, thin films and capillary waves, where surface tension competes with inertia.

Example: a spray nozzle's droplet size is set by a balance between inertia and surface tension, i.e. by $\mathrm{We}$.
Key idea: large $\mathrm{We}$ means inertia dominates; small $\mathrm{We}$ means surface tension keeps the shape.
cards.searchQuery: Weber number inertial force to surface tension droplets

cards.title: What three kinds of similarity must a model test satisfy to predict prototype behavior?
cards.body:
Geometric, kinematic and dynamic similarity.

1. **Geometric:** the model has the same shape (all length ratios equal)
2. **Kinematic:** velocities have the same direction and scaled magnitude at corresponding points
3. **Dynamic:** forces have the same ratios, which means the relevant $\Pi$ groups ($\mathrm{Re}$, $\mathrm{Fr}$, ...) are equal

Watch out: matching all dimensionless numbers at once is often impossible, which is why model tests use the dominant one and correct for the rest.
cards.searchQuery: geometric kinematic dynamic similarity model testing fluid mechanics

cards.title: A $1{:}10$ scale model is tested in the same fluid at the same temperature using Reynolds-number similarity. How many times faster than the prototype's speed must the model's flow be?
cards.body:
$10\times$.

Same $\nu$, so $\mathrm{Re}_m = \mathrm{Re}_p$ gives $V_m L_m = V_p L_p$, hence $\dfrac{V_m}{V_p} = \dfrac{L_p}{L_m} = 10$.

Watch out: that speed can be impractical (and for air models may push $\mathrm{Ma}$ near $0.3$ or above, where compressibility changes the physics).
Tip: use a different fluid (or a pressurized tunnel) to reduce the required speed.
cards.searchQuery: Reynolds number similarity scale model velocity ratio wind tunnel

cards.title: A ship is $25$ times larger than its model. With Froude-number similarity, the full-size ship travels at $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$. At what speed, in m/s, should the model be towed?
cards.body:
$2\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

$\mathrm{Fr}_m = \mathrm{Fr}_p$ gives $\dfrac{V_m}{V_p} = \sqrt{\dfrac{L_m}{L_p}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{25}} = \dfrac{1}{5}$, so $V_m = 10/5 = 2\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Why: wave-making resistance depends on gravity, so $\mathrm{Fr}$ is the governing number.
Watch out: the model's $\mathrm{Re}$ is far lower, so viscous (friction) drag must be corrected separately.
cards.searchQuery: Froude number similarity ship model speed scale 1:25

cards.title: Vortex shedding from a circular cylinder over a wide range of $\mathrm{Re}$ has a Strouhal number $\mathrm{St} = \dfrac{fD}{V}$ of approximately what value?
cards.body:
$\mathrm{St} \approx 0.2$.

So the shedding frequency is about $f \approx 0.2\,V/D$.

Example: wind at $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ past a $0.1\,\mathrm{m}$ pole sheds vortices at roughly $0.2(10)/0.1 = 20\,\mathrm{Hz}$.
Watch out: if $f$ matches a structure's natural frequency, resonance can damage chimneys, cables and bridges.
cards.searchQuery: Strouhal number vortex shedding circular cylinder 0.2

cards.title: A body has $A = 0.5\,\mathrm{m^2}$ in air ($\rho = 1.2\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$) at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and experiences $50\,\mathrm{N}$ of drag. What is $C_D$, to two decimals?
cards.body:
$C_D \approx 0.42$.

$C_D = \dfrac{F_D}{\tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2 A} = \dfrac{50}{\tfrac{1}{2}(1.2)(20)^2(0.5)} = \dfrac{50}{120} = 0.417$.

Key idea: $C_D$ is dimensionless and depends mainly on shape and $\mathrm{Re}$.
Watch out: $A$ must be the reference area the quoted $C_D$ is based on (frontal area for blunt bodies).
cards.searchQuery: drag coefficient calculation drag force dynamic pressure area

cards.title: How is the boundary-layer thickness $\delta$ conventionally defined?
cards.body:
The distance from the wall where the velocity reaches $99\%$ of the free-stream velocity, $u = 0.99\,U_\infty$.

Outside the layer the flow is nearly inviscid; inside it viscosity and no-slip matter.

Example: for laminar flow over a flat plate, $\delta \approx \dfrac{5x}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Re}_x}}$ and grows as $\sqrt{x}$.
Key idea: the layer is thin when $\mathrm{Re}$ is large.
cards.searchQuery: boundary layer thickness definition 99 percent free stream velocity

cards.title: For flow over a flat plate, at about what Reynolds number $\mathrm{Re}_x = U_\infty x/\nu$ does the boundary layer transition from laminar to turbulent?
cards.body:
$\mathrm{Re}_{x,\text{cr}} \approx 5\times10^5$.

This value depends on surface roughness, free-stream turbulence and pressure gradient. It can range from about $10^5$ to $3\times10^6$.

Why: the turbulent layer has a fuller velocity profile, so the wall shear stress and friction drag are higher after transition.
Tip: pipe flow transitions near $\mathrm{Re} \approx 2300$; don't mix up the two numbers.
cards.searchQuery: flat plate boundary layer transition critical Reynolds number 5e5

cards.title: What is the difference between friction drag and pressure (form) drag, and which dominates for a streamlined versus a bluff body?
cards.body:
Friction drag comes from wall shear stress; pressure drag comes from the pressure difference between the front and rear of the body.

**Streamlined** bodies (airfoils, fish) have mostly friction drag. **Bluff** bodies (cylinders, spheres, trucks) have mostly pressure drag, because the flow separates and leaves a low-pressure wake.

Key idea: total drag is the sum of friction drag and pressure drag.
Tip: a flat plate parallel to the flow is nearly all friction; turned perpendicular to the flow, it's nearly all pressure drag.
cards.searchQuery: friction drag versus pressure drag streamlined bluff body

cards.title: What causes boundary-layer separation on a body?
cards.body:
An adverse pressure gradient: pressure increasing in the flow direction, $\dfrac{dP}{dx} > 0$.

The fluid near the wall has little momentum, so it can't push against rising pressure and stops, then reverses, so the layer detaches (where the wall shear is zero).

Why: the result is a wide, low-pressure wake, which causes large pressure drag.
Tip: a turbulent boundary layer has more near-wall momentum, so it resists separation longer than a laminar one.
cards.searchQuery: boundary layer separation adverse pressure gradient cause wake

cards.title: State Stokes' drag law for a sphere of diameter $D$ moving at speed $V$ through a fluid of viscosity $\mu$, and when it applies.
cards.body:
$F_D = 3\pi\mu V D$, valid for creeping flow with $\mathrm{Re} = \dfrac{\rho V D}{\mu} < 1$.

In this regime inertia is negligible and the drag is purely viscous, so $F_D$ is **linear** in $V$ (not quadratic).

Example: a fine dust particle or oil droplet settling in air or water is a Stokes-flow problem.
Watch out: at higher $\mathrm{Re}$ the drag grows faster than linearly and the $\tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2 C_D A$ form is used instead.
cards.searchQuery: Stokes drag law sphere 3 pi mu V D creeping flow Reynolds number below 1

cards.title: A parachutist's total weight is $864\,\mathrm{N}$, with $\rho = 1.2\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ and $C_D A = 1.6\,\mathrm{m^2}$. What is the terminal velocity, in m/s? (Neglect buoyancy.)
cards.body:
$30\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

At terminal velocity, drag equals weight: $\tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2 C_D A = W$, so $V = \sqrt{\dfrac{2W}{\rho\,C_D A}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(864)}{(1.2)(1.6)}} = \sqrt{900} = 30\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Why: net force is zero, so the acceleration stops.
Watch out: for a body in a liquid (or any fluid dense enough), include the buoyant force in the balance.
cards.searchQuery: terminal velocity drag equals weight parachute calculation

cards.title: A wing has $C_L = 1.0$ and $A = 20\,\mathrm{m^2}$ in air ($\rho = 1.2\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$) at $50\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is the lift, in kN?
cards.body:
$30\,\mathrm{kN}$.

$F_L = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2 C_L A = \tfrac{1}{2}(1.2)(50)^2(1.0)(20) = 30{,}000\,\mathrm{N}$.

Key idea: lift grows as $V^2$, so a plane must be faster to keep the same lift when flying at lower density (higher altitude) or with a smaller $C_L$.
Tip: for wings, $A$ is the planform area.
cards.searchQuery: lift force equation wing C_L planform area calculation

cards.title: What is aerodynamic stall of a wing, and why does lift drop?
cards.body:
At a large angle of attack the flow separates from the upper surface, and lift falls sharply while drag rises.

Lift grows with angle of attack until the **adverse pressure gradient** on the upper surface separates the boundary layer; past that, $C_L$ drops.

Watch out: stall depends on angle of attack, not on airspeed; a plane can stall at any speed if the angle is large enough.
Tip: flaps and slats delay stall at low speeds by keeping the flow attached or raising $C_{L,\max}$.
cards.searchQuery: aerodynamic stall angle of attack flow separation lift drop

cards.title: What is the drag crisis for a sphere, and why do golf balls have dimples?
cards.body:
The sphere's $C_D$ drops sharply near $\mathrm{Re} \approx 2$ to $4\times10^5$ because the boundary layer turns turbulent.

The turbulent layer separates **later**, making the wake narrower and cutting pressure drag. Dimples trip the layer to turbulence at lower speeds, so the ball flies in the low-drag regime.

Key idea: roughness can reduce drag on bluff bodies, even though it raises friction drag.
Watch out: for streamlined bodies, roughness only increases drag.
cards.searchQuery: drag crisis sphere turbulent boundary layer golf ball dimples

cards.title: How is the operating point of a pump in a piping system found?
cards.body:
At the intersection of the pump curve and the system curve.

The **pump curve** gives head $H$ versus flow rate $Q$ (falling with $Q$). The **system curve** is $H = H_{\text{static}} + K Q^2$, the head needed to lift the water and overcome friction (rising with $Q$).

Why: only at the intersection do the head the pump supplies and the head the system requires match.
Tip: a throttling valve raises $K$, steepening the system curve and lowering the flow.
cards.searchQuery: pump curve system curve intersection operating point head flow rate

cards.title: To avoid cavitation in a pump, must the available net positive suction head (NPSH) be greater or smaller than the required NPSH?
cards.body:
Greater.

$\mathrm{NPSH_A}$ is the head of the liquid at the pump inlet above its vapor pressure head: $\mathrm{NPSH_A} = \dfrac{P_{\text{inlet}}}{\rho g} + \dfrac{V^2}{2g} - \dfrac{P_v}{\rho g}$. $\mathrm{NPSH_R}$ is the manufacturer's minimum.

Why: if $\mathrm{NPSH_A} < \mathrm{NPSH_R}$, the local pressure inside the pump falls below the vapor pressure and bubbles form.
Tip: lower the pump, shorten or enlarge the suction pipe, or cool the liquid to raise $\mathrm{NPSH_A}$.
cards.searchQuery: NPSH available greater than required pump cavitation

cards.title: A pump's speed rises from $1000$ to $1500\,\mathrm{rpm}$ (same impeller and a similar operating point). By what factor does the head change?
cards.body:
$2.25\times$.

Affinity laws: $Q \propto N$ and $H \propto N^2$, so $H_2/H_1 = (1500/1000)^2 = 2.25$.

Example: the flow rate rises by $1.5\times$ at the same time.
Watch out: the laws assume the same impeller diameter and fluid, and a similar operating point (same efficiency).
cards.searchQuery: pump affinity laws head proportional to speed squared

cards.title: A pump's speed rises from $1000$ to $1500\,\mathrm{rpm}$ (same impeller and a similar operating point). By what factor does the shaft power change?
cards.body:
$3.375\times$ (about $3.4$).

Affinity laws: $\dot{W} \propto N^3$, so $\dot{W}_2/\dot{W}_1 = (1.5)^3 = 3.375$.

Why: power $\propto \rho g Q H \propto N \cdot N^2$.
Key idea: a modest speed increase demands a large power increase, and a modest speed cut saves a lot of energy.
cards.searchQuery: pump affinity laws power proportional to speed cubed

cards.title: A pump delivers $10\,\mathrm{L/s}$ of water at $30\,\mathrm{m}$ of head using $4.2\,\mathrm{kW}$ of shaft power. What is its efficiency, in percent?
cards.body:
$70\%$.

Water power $= \rho g Q H = (1000)(9.81)(0.01)(30) = 2943\,\mathrm{W}$, so $\eta = \dfrac{2943}{4200} = 0.70$.

Tip: $10\,\mathrm{L/s} = 0.01\,\mathrm{m^3/s}$.
Watch out: efficiency is output (water power) divided by input (shaft power), never the reverse.
cards.searchQuery: pump efficiency water power divided by shaft power calculation

cards.title: A hydroelectric turbine receives $2\,\mathrm{m^3/s}$ of water at a net head of $50\,\mathrm{m}$ with $90\%$ efficiency. Power output, in kW to the nearest whole number?
cards.body:
$883\,\mathrm{kW}$.

$\dot{W} = \eta\,\rho g Q H = (0.90)(1000)(9.81)(2)(50) = 882{,}900\,\mathrm{W}$.

Key idea: for turbines, shaft power is **less** than the water power, so $\eta$ multiplies; for pumps it divides.
Watch out: "net head" already excludes pipe losses; if given the gross head, subtract $h_L$ first.
cards.searchQuery: hydroelectric turbine power eta rho g Q H net head calculation

cards.title: Speed of sound in air at $300\,\mathrm{K}$ ($k = 1.4$, $R = 287\,\mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)}$), in m/s to the nearest whole number?
cards.body:
$347\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

$c = \sqrt{kRT} = \sqrt{(1.4)(287)(300)} = \sqrt{120{,}540} = 347\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Why: sound is a nearly isentropic pressure wave, so $c^2 = (\partial P/\partial\rho)_s = kRT$ for an ideal gas.
Watch out: $T$ must be in kelvins, and $R$ in $\mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)}$ so that $c$ comes out in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
cards.searchQuery: speed of sound ideal gas sqrt(kRT) air 300 K

cards.title: An aircraft flies at $250\,\mathrm{m/s}$ where the speed of sound is $340\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is its Mach number, to two decimals?
cards.body:
$\mathrm{Ma} \approx 0.74$.

$\mathrm{Ma} = \dfrac{V}{c} = \dfrac{250}{340} = 0.735$.

Key idea: at $\mathrm{Ma} = 0.74$ the flow is subsonic but compressible (above $0.3$), and shock waves may start to form on parts of the wing, near the critical Mach number.
Tip: for gases, always compute $\mathrm{Ma}$ with the local $T$.
cards.searchQuery: Mach number calculation flight speed divided by speed of sound

cards.title: In a converging nozzle, what is the exit Mach number once the flow is choked?
cards.body:
$\mathrm{Ma} = 1$ (sonic) at the exit.

Choked flow means the mass flow rate has reached its maximum: lowering the back pressure further doesn't increase it.

Why: information about downstream pressure travels at the speed of sound, so it can't travel upstream against a sonic exit.
Tip: a converging-diverging nozzle is needed to accelerate the flow beyond $\mathrm{Ma} = 1$.
cards.searchQuery: choked flow converging nozzle exit Mach number 1 maximum mass flow

cards.title: What is open-channel flow with Froude number $\mathrm{Fr} < 1$ called?
cards.body:
Subcritical flow.

It's deep and slow, and surface waves can travel upstream because they move faster than the flow.

For $\mathrm{Fr} > 1$ the flow is **supercritical** (shallow and fast), and for $\mathrm{Fr} = 1$ it is critical.
Key idea: a hydraulic jump is the abrupt transition from supercritical to subcritical flow, with significant energy loss.
cards.searchQuery: open channel flow subcritical Froude number less than 1

cards.title: State Manning's equation for the mean velocity in an open channel (SI units).
cards.body:
$V = \dfrac{1}{n}\,R_h^{2/3}\,S^{1/2}$

Here $n$ is the Manning roughness coefficient, $R_h = A/P$ is the hydraulic radius ($A$ the flow area, $P$ the wetted perimeter) and $S$ is the channel slope.

Example: $n \approx 0.013$ for smooth concrete and about $0.035$ for a natural earth channel.
Watch out: with US units the constant $1/n$ becomes $1.49/n$.
cards.searchQuery: Manning equation open channel velocity hydraulic radius slope roughness

cards.title: A rectangular open channel is $2\,\mathrm{m}$ wide and carries water $1\,\mathrm{m}$ deep. What is the hydraulic radius $R_h$, in m?
cards.body:
$0.5\,\mathrm{m}$.

$A = 2(1) = 2\,\mathrm{m^2}$ and the wetted perimeter is the bottom plus two sides, $P = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4\,\mathrm{m}$, so $R_h = A/P = 0.5\,\mathrm{m}$.

Watch out: the free surface is **not** part of the wetted perimeter.
Tip: for a very wide channel, $R_h \to$ the depth $y$.
cards.searchQuery: hydraulic radius rectangular open channel A over P wetted perimeter
